title: PAUL CHANGED HIS STRATEGY—BUT HE REFUSED TO CHANGE THIS ONE THING
paragraphs: PAUL CHANGED HIS STRATEGY—BUT HE REFUSED TO CHANGE THIS ONE THING

Why the apostle could reason in a synagogue, speak differently to pagans, quote poets in Athens, become “all things to all people,” and still preach the same crucified and risen Christ—and what his missionary fire exposes about the way we carry the Gospel today.
There is something almost unsettling about Paul.
Put him in a synagogue, and he sounds like a Jewish Bible teacher.
Put him among Gentiles who barely understand Israel’s Scriptures, and he begins somewhere else.
Put him before philosophers in Athens, and he talks about creation, humanity, repentance, judgment, and resurrection.
Put him among the broken, immoral, spiritually confused people of Corinth, and he plants his feet at the foot of a bloody cross.
Put him in prison, and somehow the prison becomes another pulpit.
Change the audience, and Paul may change his doorway.
But he refuses to change the destination.
And once you see it, one sentence Paul wrote becomes almost impossible to forget:
“τοῖς πᾶσιν γέγονα πάντα, ἵνα πάντως τινὰς σώσω.”
Tois pasin gegona panta, hina pantōs tinas sōsō.
“I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.”
Paul did not say, “I changed the truth so people would accept me.”
He did not say, “I removed whatever offended the culture.”
He did not say, “I discovered which message performed best and preached that instead.”
He said he became “all things to all people.”
“γέγονα πάντα” carries the sense, “I have become all things.”
“So that by all means I might save some.”
Not make some admire his intelligence.
Paul was willing to change himself before he would change Christ.
And that may be where this story stops being merely about Paul and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because sometimes we do the opposite.
We protect our comfort and modify our witness.
Paul protected the Gospel and modified his approach.
Watch him enter Pisidian Antioch in Acts 13.
He enters the synagogue. His listeners know Israel’s history. They understand Abraham, Moses, David, the prophets, and the expectation of God’s Messiah.
So Paul does not begin by proving that there is a God.
He begins inside the biblical story his audience already knows.
He walks through Israel’s history and brings them toward David, then toward Jesus.
Then watch what happens in Acts 14.
Paul and Barnabas are in Lystra when a man unable to walk is healed. The crowd becomes so overwhelmed that they conclude the missionaries must be gods in human form.
Suddenly Paul is not dealing primarily with synagogue listeners trained in the Hebrew Scriptures.
He tells them to turn from “vain things” to the living God who made heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them.
Notice what Paul does not do.
He does not begin with a long explanation of Davidic kingship to people who do not share the necessary biblical framework.
He begins with something they can understand:
The evidence of divine generosity surrounding their ordinary lives.
But he has no intention of leaving them there.
Acts 17 describes a city filled with idols.
Paul enters the synagogue, but he also reasons in the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers encounter him. Eventually he stands before the Areopagus.
And Paul does something that still makes Christians argue about missionary strategy two thousand years later.
He begins with something he observed in their city.
Paul does not affirm Athenian idolatry as another legitimate road to God. Acts explicitly tells us that his spirit was provoked because the city was full of idols.
He understands enough about his audience to build a bridge from what they recognize toward what they desperately need to know.
Then he proclaims the God who made the world.
The Lord of heaven and earth.
The One who does not live in temples made by human hands.
The One from whom humanity receives life and breath.
Paul even draws upon language familiar from Greek poetry.
That does not mean Paul surrendered biblical revelation to pagan philosophy.
It means Paul could recognize a fragment of truth in his listeners’ cultural world and use it as a bridge toward the fuller truth they did not yet possess.
Then the bridge reaches somewhere uncomfortable.
Acts 17:30 says that God “commands all people everywhere to repent.”
Paul has not softened the Gospel.
He has contextualized his communication without surrendering his conviction.
That is important because successful evangelism in Scripture is not measured by whether everybody likes the preacher.
He did not manipulate the outcome.
He proclaimed truth and left the human response before God.
Because we live in an age obsessed with attention.
And none of those things are inherently evil.
A missionary can use a road.
A missionary can use a ship.
A Christian today can use a microphone, a book, a video, Facebook, a website, or whatever legitimate means allows truth to travel farther.
Paul understood something the Church must never forget:
Contextualization is not compromise when the message remains faithful to Christ.
But contextualization becomes compromise the moment we begin removing biblical truth because we are ashamed of how people might respond to it.
And Paul knew exactly where that line was.
Listen to him writing to Corinth:
“οὐ γὰρ ἔκρινά τι εἰδέναι ἐν ὑμῖν εἰ μὴ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον.”
Ou gar ekrina ti eidenai en hymin ei mē Iēsoun Christon kai touton estaurōmenon.
“For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.”
Paul could speak differently in Athens than he did in a synagogue.
He could work with his hands.
He could address Jews, Gentiles, philosophers, governors, prisoners, merchants, soldiers, and ordinary families.
But beneath every legitimate adaptation stood an unmovable scandal:
And Paul knew it was scandalous.
Earlier in the same letter he writes:
You cannot stand beneath it and keep pretending you saved yourself.
You cannot stare at the crucified Christ and still believe sin is merely a minor personality defect.
The cross tells you something went terribly wrong with humanity.
And then it tells you something unimaginably beautiful about God.
We accumulated guilt we could never erase by religious performance.
And death did not get the final word.
This is why Paul’s missionary flexibility never became theological flexibility.
If salvation were merely self-improvement, Paul could have redesigned the message for every market.
But Paul believed something had actually happened in history.
Paul summarizes this in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 and identifies it as something of “first importance.”
Christianity was not Paul selling spiritual inspiration.
The Greek word so closely associated with this proclamation is εὐαγγέλιον—euangelion—good news, Gospel.
News cannot be faithfully improved by changing what happened.
But if you change the event itself, you no longer have the same news.
That is why Paul changed mission strategies.
Not because he was uncertain about the Gospel.
Because he was certain about it.
He cared enough about people to ask:
How can I remove unnecessary barriers without removing the necessary offense of the cross?
How can I speak so this person actually understands what I mean?
How can I enter their world without allowing their world to redefine Jesus?
How can I meet them where they are without pretending where they are is where God intends them to remain?
And it is much harder than simply shouting religious vocabulary at people who do not understand it.
It requires knowing Scripture deeply enough to distinguish the eternal message from our preferred method of presenting it.
Paul explains his heartbeat in 1 Corinthians 9:19:
“Though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them.”
He was not asking, “What makes ministry easiest for me?”
He was asking, “What might help me reach them?”
There is a frightening question hidden inside that sentence for every Christian reading this.
When was the last time you inconvenienced yourself because somebody needed Jesus?
Not when did you post a verse.
Not when did you win an argument.

When did another person’s soul become heavy enough on your heart that you were willing to listen to their questions, understand their wounds, speak their language, sit through their doubts, pray through their resistance, and patiently point them toward Christ?
Maybe the person you have been arguing with does not need another argument tonight.
Maybe they need to see Jesus in the way you listen.
Maybe your unbelieving child knows your political opinions better than they know the tenderness of Christ through you.
Maybe your spouse has heard your Bible verses but rarely hears you say, “Forgive me.”
Maybe the person at work you quietly judged is carrying a private grief you never bothered to understand.
Maybe somebody on your Facebook friends list has been watching your life while silently wondering whether Christianity could possibly have anything for people like them.
Paul’s missionary strategy asks us to stop seeing audiences.
People made in the image of God.
People carrying histories you cannot see.
People scrolling at two in the morning because sleep will not come.
People who know church language but have forgotten what grace feels like.
People who walked away after being wounded.
People who look successful while privately falling apart.
People who believe their scandal is too filthy for Jesus.
And perhaps that last person is you.
Maybe you clicked this article expecting history.
But somewhere along the way, something became personal.
Because you have spent years changing strategies too.
When to hide the browser history.
When to promise God, “This is the last time.”
When to sing at church while carrying something nobody sitting beside you knows.
You learned how to look spiritually alive while becoming exhausted inside.
And now the cross is standing in front of you.
This is where the Gospel becomes scandalous grace.
Jesus did not come for the edited version of you.
The questions you are afraid to say aloud.
And the answer of Christianity is not that sin does not matter.
The cross proves that it matters more than we want to admit.
But the cross also proves that God’s grace reaches farther than repentant sinners dare imagine.
Jesus Christ receives sinners who turn to Him.
Not because tears pay the debt.
Not because religious improvement earns another chance.
And repentance means we stop defending the darkness and turn toward Him.
Maybe that is why you needed to read about Paul changing missionary strategies today.
Because God has been pursuing people through unexpected doorways for a very long time.
And perhaps, tonight, an article appearing on your screen.
So stop running because you think your scandal gets the final sentence.
Peter’s denial did not write the final sentence of Peter.
Paul’s persecution of Christians did not write the final sentence of Paul.
The thief’s criminal past did not get the final word at the cross.
And Jesus Christ still rewrites human stories.
Turn from the sin you have been protecting.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And if your heart is exhausted and you need brothers and sisters to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
If you have been fighting your way back toward Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”

If grace has already reached into something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the doorway through which another wounded person finally believes that restoration is possible.
That is one lesson Paul’s missionary life leaves us with.
Use whatever faithful doorway God has placed in front of you.
But when you walk through it, bring them Jesus.
Not because Christians must financially support Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
Scripture gives us no right to make such a claim.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and Christian giving is to be willing rather than coerced; as 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should not be “reluctantly or under compulsion.”
But voluntary support can become one practical expression of partnership in Gospel work.
Then do something Paul would understand immediately.
Do not keep the message inside the room.
Send it privately to someone struggling.
Follow not merely because you want more content.
Stay close because in a world endlessly competing to disciple your attention, you need truth continually bringing your eyes back to Christ.
And remember why Paul could change strategies without losing himself.
His identity was not anchored to a strategy.
His identity was anchored to Jesus.
He could preach in a synagogue today and reason in a marketplace tomorrow.
He could quote Scripture to one audience and begin with creation before another.
He could become weak to the weak.
He could become all things to all people.
And perhaps that is the word the modern Church desperately needs.
Do not worship yesterday’s strategy or tomorrow’s technology.
Use whatever is lawful, wise, loving, and faithful.
Understand the people in front of you.
But when the doorway finally opens...
Not a Christ redesigned to fit the spirit of the age.
Jesus Christ calling sinners to repentance.
Jesus Christ transforming those who trust Him.
That was Paul’s mission beneath all his changing strategies.
So be honest before you leave.
Did this article merely teach you something about Paul...
or did God expose something about you?
Follow because your soul needs more than endless scrolling.
Paul changed the doorway because he loved the people.
He never changed the destination because only Jesus could save them.
And when your worst chapter whispers that your story is already over, remember this:
The scandal may explain how you arrived at the cross—but grace decides who walks away from it forgiven.
